item.title: The Dad Nobody Screens For
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

The Dad Nobody Screens For

Our story of paternal postpartum depression, and the research that came from it.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Fathers face real risk for postpartum depression, but often are not screened.
  • "Masked male depression" can look like withdrawal, irritability, or heavy sleep instead of tears or sadness.
  • Research found 27 risk factors and 21 protective factors, and the most protective ones center on connection.

Rewind to 15 years ago. I had given birth to our first child, our daughter. The birth itself…didn't go as planned. I went into it with some rigid ideas of how I wanted things to go — my protector parts trying to gain control in an experience that made me nervous. The image that took a long time to heal from was when they finally pulled her out during the emergency cesarean; my husband said, "Look, Cassidy, she's here!" And I turned away, my eyes closed.

The exhaustion. The medication. And the shame. My eyes wouldn't open. I turned away from both of them. That moment, oof, it was sticky.

I didn't protect any space to process it. It was time to ace the next "project" of parenthood — exclusive breastfeeding, the "perfect" sleep routine, optimizing every waking moment face to face with our daughter. Can you sense my inner perfectionist parts at the postpartum wheel? Oh yeah, they were.

I talk about healing those parts of myself and becoming a less reactive, more connected, and present parent in my book Mom Needs a Moment. But this article is about a different part of the story.

The shame and resentment

My husband got the first five words of my book: "'What the hell,' Dave muttered." I'd been up all night with our daughter again (anxiety didn't allow me to "sleep when the baby sleeps"). She'd just had a flying feces situation, and as it dripped down the white curtains of her nursery, my husband trudged in, wiping the sleepies from his eyes.

Did I resent him for the sleep he was getting? Yes. Was I consumed with shame over my intrusive anxious thoughts, and my own desire to escape? Also yes.

But there's a story I don't dive into as deeply in the book: my husband's postpartum depression.

The question no one asked him

I was assessed for postpartum depression, thank goodness — though not for postpartum anxiety, what I was later diagnosed with. My husband was screened for neither. At the time, that seemed normal?! This was 2011 — no one was talking about non-birthing partners being at risk postpartum. When providers turned to me, they asked about my symptoms. When they turned to him, they asked, "Are you helping?", which, at the time, also seemed right. Mothers absolutely take the brunt of household and parenting labor — we can blame the patriarchy in the air we breathe. But patriarchy hurts men too: toughness asked for over tenderness, no room for vulnerability, no model for how to ask for help and be present for yourself and your family.

He was depressed — the birth of our child was the trigger. Of course, non-birthing partners are also at risk — identities shift, sleep is broken, and it turns out, there are plenty of other reasons.

It took time to admit that we were both struggling. It was messy behind closed doors for a while. But when those wounds scarred over through support, I became determined to move the needle for other families.

I went back for my doctorate when our daughter was one. When it was time to choose my dissertation research, I knew what I wanted to explore — our experience became the muse.

What I went looking for

I designed an international Delphi study that was later published in the Journal of Affective Disorders— a method where experts cycle answers back to each other, round after round, until consensus emerges. My panel consisted of physicians, psychologists, and family therapists across multiple countries, all working with fathers in the perinatal period. I wasn't trying to prove paternal depression was real…we knew it was. I wanted to know why we couldn't agree on what it was — and why caring, competent professionals could screen one parent thoroughly and ask the other to simply be "helpful."

The research reflected what we had experienced. Finally, the panel helped name it: masked male depression. If you ask clinicians to describe postpartum depression in a mother, you actually get quite a bit of overlap — tearfulness, hopelessness, disrupted bonding, guilt. But ask them to describe it in a father, and the picture blurs a bit. Some describe classic symptoms. But sometimes it looks nothing like the textbook checklist — irritability, withdrawal, a sudden uptick in drinking or overworking, a restless kind of escape.

What I found

The experts in my study reached consensus on several risk factors for postpartum depression in dads. The strongest risk factors included a personal or family history of mood or anxiety disorders, poor social support, and a partner who is also struggling with depression or anxiety. Turns out that paternal and maternal mental health are deeply intertwined (something I lived before I saw it in the data).

This group of international experts also identified protective factors, and almost all of them were about relationships and belonging, such as: a strong partner relationship, open communication about fear and doubt (not just logistics), being actively included in caregiving from the start, employers who support paternity leave and don't punish the priority of being a father, and a sense of meaning in the transition.

When I asked what depression actually feels like for a postpartum father, the words that came forward weren't just "sad" or "hopeless." The themes that emerged were: confusion about how to father, a gap between the man he thought he'd be and what was showing up, missing parts of his old life, feeling trapped, and also a creeping, sinking sense of inadequacy.

The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (the standard screener) wasn't exactly built to look for this experience of postpartum, and it's hard to detect these symptoms when the only question a father is asked is "are you helping?"

This is what that first year with our baby, and later the dissertation, taught me: We need to be looking at the whole family system postpartum. When a father struggles silently — because no one screened for it, because "masked" depression looks like withdrawal instead of tears — that struggle moves through the whole household. It shapes how supported a mother feels. I can tell you firsthand, it does.

So now I always ask a dad about his sleep. I ask how he experienced the birth. I ask how he's doing with the transition, not just how he's helping. Often a partner is the one to see the shift — the irritability, the withdrawal, the extra hour at the office — long before any screening tool would. So, I always check in with them too.

The absence of tears is not the absence of depression. Struggling to bond doesn't mean he doesn't love this baby. And "I don't really know how to be a dad right now" isn't weakness...it may be the most useful sentence he can say out loud to a partner, a friend, or someone trained to hear it.

As a society, we still miss the mark for moms' and dads' mental health. But almost fifteen years later, I know we don't need perfect marks to start asking better questions — at home, and in every exam room where a new father sits quietly beside the parent most people now remember to ask about.

item.title: What Visions and Emotions Can We Expect Just Before Dying?
item.description:
Near-Death Experiences

What Visions and Emotions Can We Expect Just Before Dying?

A new theory of near-death experiences builds on past models, but adds a twist.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Past research on near-death experiences has identified key patterns in brain activity and perceptions.
  • Survivors overwhelmingly report positive emotions, such as feeling peaceful.
  • The newly proposed dying-moment dream hypothesis highlights the individual’s emotional history.
What will your end-of-life visions be?
Source: #2194100587/by Deagreez/iStock.com

In the movie Ghost Town, Ricky Gervais’ character finds out he’d temporarily died during a routine procedure—and the hospital staff hadn’t told him. He confronts his surgeon, played by Kristen Wiig:

Wiig: “Everybody dies.”

Gervais: “Yeah, but usually at the end of their life, and just the once…”

Many of us assume death is a one-time deal. Yet, millions report coming surprisingly close. In a survey across 35 countries, the prevalence rate for near-death experiences (NDEs) was 10%.

What Happens in Your Dying Moments?

One surprising discovery is that as we expire, the brain doesn’t shut down all at once. A study of dying comatose patients showed a cascade of activity in different brain areas.

Researchers are working to match these neural changes to what the person reports feeling and thinking. Of course, they can’t do that with people who “don’t make the return flight.”

But some do make it back.

What Do People Recount From NDEs?

Many studies show common themes, including a peaceful feeling, a bright light, a meeting with another being, clear thinking, a dark place, an altered sense of time, and a return to the living.

Here's an example of a prototypical memory:

I left my body and saw people in scrubs working on me. Then, I floated toward a bright light. I reunited with my grandmother. I’m thinking, “I’m dead. This is awesome!” Someone said I must go back, and suddenly I was in the hospital.

The Good News: Most People Report Pleasant Emotions

The vast majority of NDE descriptions convey a happy finale.

Researchers in France and Belgium found that feelings of peace dominated the experience. Many also reported suddenly understanding everything and feeling joy.

In a multi-site study of cardiac arrest survivors, some patients reported feeling overwhelming peace and love during the time in which they were receiving CPR.

These findings suggest that the soundtrack for our final exit should be upbeat—more like Louis Armstrong's What a Wonderful World than The Rolling Stones’ Paint It Black.

The not quite so good news is that, for some, the near death experience is a bad trip. In one sample, 14% recalled distressing features.

A New Theory: The Dying-Moment Dream Hypothesis

The remarkable similarities across NDE memories have inspired scientists to look at biological explanations. Can we link changes in brain activity to people’s NDE reports?

Convincing theories have been published — for example, the NEPTUNE model (Neurophysiological Evolutionary Psychological Theory Understanding Near-death Experience).

But recently, a new theory emerged. It builds on past models but adds a few intriguing claims.

According to the dying-moment dream hypothesis, proposed by Kayış, the movie reel that plays near the end of life is best explained as a dream-like state our brains create.

The chain of events begins when the brain becomes deprived of oxygen, such as during cardiac arrest. This is followed by a surge in gamma waves and a flood of feel-good neurotransmitters, including serotonin.

At some point, input from the outside world—from our eyes, ears, etc.—is cut off, and the brain only produces thoughts and feelings from within. Our life memories spew out.

But they are not randomly sampled. Instead, the individual’s emotional life history determines the tone of the imagery—whether it’s comforting scenes or a horror show. Someone who has endured trauma or unresolved guilt will likely experience distressing—even hellish—thoughts near death. Someone with a history of secure attachments and love can look forward to a blissful state.

Cultural and religious backgrounds also shape NDE narratives. For instance, in Christian cultures, the bright light is seen as a being of light, but in Japan, it’s an inanimate object—maybe just a really bright light.

Many, many elements of this new theory of NDEs have had starring roles in earlier models, including gamma surges, cascading brain activity, memory activation, cultural influences, and similarities between dreaming and NDEs.

Fact Checking: Does the Evidence Line up With the New Theory?

Many of the mechanisms proposed in the dying-moment dream hypothesis are indeed grounded in evidence. Older, more established theories also incorporated these robust scientific findings. For instance, EEG studies of patients near death have shown brain activity that looks like the patterns observed in memory retrieval.

But some claims in the dying-moment dream hypothesis remain speculative.

The biggest unanswered question involves the driving force of a person’s predominant emotional history.

In this theory, the person’s accumulated emotional past—for example, having had a life defined by love or moral guilt—determines whether the end-of-life experience will be pleasant or hellish.

Visions of heaven or hell? That seems like an effect most people would be interested in, to put it mildly. Is there evidence to back it up?

No. Although intriguing, this idea is untested.

In sum, the new theory pulls together scholarship from a variety of fields. However, newly suggested components still await empirical testing.

What to Expect When You’re Expiring

Source: #1076746334/by czarny_bez/iStock.com

So, what will you experience in an NDE (and perhaps as the lights go out permanently)?

Well, it might be nothing at all. Less than 40% of people report having any conscious experience. A study of ICU patients put the number even lower, at 15%.

If you do have an NDE, chances are you’ll bask in feelings of peace, love, and understanding. Wait. Are our last moments like an Elvis Costello song?

I guess that’s as good a way as any to go out.
